title: Drift-Constrained Optimization: Only Direction Matters in Fine-Tuning Instruct Models
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 12 Sep 2026]
    Title:Drift-Constrained Optimization: Only Direction Matters in Fine-Tuning Instruct Models
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Fine-tuning instruct models often improves target performance while inducing behavioral drift from the reference model, which can degrade existing capabilities. Rather than treating this drift as an uncontrolled consequence of optimization, we specify a behavioral drift budget before optimization and ask how to boost the target-task performance within it. Locally, behavioral drift induces a shared geometry anchored at the reference model, with the drift budget defining a boundary within this space. In this space, drift determines distance from the reference, leaving update direction as the remaining degree of freedom. Fine-tuning updates can therefore be compared through their directional efficiency, naturally reformulating fine-tuning as a direction-selection problem. This reformulation makes a concrete prediction: changing the accessible directions can qualitatively alter the outcome of fine-tuning. We test this prediction in a stringent QA-only setting, where strong instruct models are fine-tuned only on final answers but must still generate multi-step reasoning at inference. Despite this mismatch, a coarse layer-selective probe reverses the failure of QA-only fine-tuning and reveals the existence of effective directions, with multiple neighboring configurations improving target performance while preserving reasoning and general capabilities. Across Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, these directions substantially improve scientific reasoning and multilingual translation. Over more than 100 languages, the resulting models match or outperform dedicated translation systems and provide a stronger initialization for subsequent reinforcement learning. Our results suggest that fine-tuning is not just about how much a model changes, but how that change is spent. this https URL and this https URL

report.summary: New research shows fine-tuning outcomes depend on the direction of weight updates, not their size, letting models learn new skills without losing existing ones.
report.background: Fine-tuning an instruct model on a narrow dataset — support transcripts, math answers, translation pairs — routinely boosts the target task while quietly eroding everything else. Practitioners call it catastrophic forgetting; alignment researchers call it the alignment tax. Standard fixes are blunt: mix in replay data, lower the learning rate, freeze layers, or add KL penalties that cap how far the model may stray from its reference checkpoint. All of these treat drift as a cost to be minimized, and none answers what the model should change instead. Meanwhile post-training has become the main battleground for frontier labs, where targeted fine-tuning or reinforcement learning decides benchmark leadership. That makes the geometry of updates — not just their magnitude — scientifically and commercially important.
key_points: Drift as a budget, not a side effect: instead of measuring how much a model drifted after training, you declare a drift budget up front — a boundary around the reference model — then ask which update direction buys the most task improvement inside it. Locally, drift fixes distance, leaving direction as the only free variable.

This turns fine-tuning into a direction-selection problem. Updates can be ranked by 'directional efficiency' — gain per unit of drift — and the authors predict that merely changing which directions are reachable should qualitatively change results. Parameterization matters more than step size or epoch count.

They test it in a deliberately hostile setting: fine-tuning strong instruct models on final answers only, with no reasoning traces, while still demanding multi-step chain-of-thought at inference. Standard QA-only fine-tuning breaks reasoning; a coarse layer-selective probe reverses that failure, proving effective directions exist.

On Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B these directions substantially improve scientific reasoning and multilingual translation. Over 100+ languages the resulting models match or beat dedicated translation systems despite no translation-specific tuning, and they are a stronger initialization for later reinforcement learning.

The takeaway: 'fine-tuning is not just about how much a model changes, but how that change is spent.' Capability loss is often a bad-direction problem rather than an unavoidable capacity trade-off, reframing how teams budget and evaluate post-training runs.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this shifts post-training from heuristic data-mixing toward direction-aware optimization: smaller, cheaper specialization runs with less replay data and fewer alignment-tax trade-offs. For developers, the practical win is cost — a coarse layer-selective probe is inexpensive and works with existing LoRA-style pipelines, suggesting drift should be tracked as an explicit budget alongside benchmark deltas. For users, it hints at models that absorb domain skills without regressing reasoning, stronger multilingual translation straight from general checkpoints, and fewer surprise capability drops after an app update. Caveats remain: the shared local geometry is an assumption, results are shown mainly on the Qwen3 family, and independent replication is still needed.
report.tools: To follow up, watch Hugging Face PEFT (LoRA/DoRA) and torchtune for direction- and layer-selective updates, TRL for KL-regularized RL comparisons and later RL stages, Axolotl or Unsloth for cheap fine-tuning runs, and lm-evaluation-harness or lighteval for measuring the skill-versus-drift frontier. vLLM helps serve both reference and tuned checkpoints for side-by-side regression testing. The paper's linked code is the best starting point for reproducing the layer-selective probe.
